definition: The resistance of tissue to the propagation of ultrasound waves, calculated as the product of tissue density and sound propagation speed.
As Low As Reasonably Achievable - the practice of minimizing ultrasound exposure while obtaining diagnostic information.
A Doppler artifact that occurs when blood flow velocity exceeds the Nyquist limit, causing the signal to wrap around and display in the wrong direction.
The progressive weakening of ultrasound intensity as it travels through tissue, caused by absorption, reflection, and scattering.
The ability to distinguish two structures along the beam axis, primarily determined by spatial pulse length and frequency.
A reverberation artifact appearing as closely spaced echoes extending deep to a strong reflector.
The change in frequency of ultrasound waves reflected from moving blood cells, proportional to the velocity of flow.
The region where the ultrasound beam is narrowest and lateral resolution is best.
The number of complete images displayed per second, typically measured in frames per second (fps) or Hertz (Hz).
The number of sound wave cycles per second, measured in Hertz (Hz). Higher frequencies provide better resolution but less penetration.
Amplification of returning echo signals to improve image brightness without changing the transmitted power.
The ability to distinguish two structures perpendicular to the beam axis, determined by beam width.
A duplication artifact where structures appear on both sides of a strong reflector, commonly seen at the diaphragm.
The maximum Doppler shift frequency that can be accurately detected, equal to half the pulse repetition frequency.
The property of certain crystals to convert electrical energy into mechanical vibrations (sound waves) and vice versa.
A Doppler technique that displays the amplitude of Doppler signals rather than frequency shift, more sensitive to slow flow.
The number of ultrasound pulses transmitted per second, determines maximum depth and Doppler velocity range.
Multiple equally-spaced echoes caused by ultrasound bouncing back and forth between two strong reflectors.
An artifact appearing as a dark area behind highly attenuating or reflecting structures like calcifications.
Depth-dependent amplification that compensates for attenuation, producing uniform brightness throughout the image.
